Begin by asking for the locality if it has not been supplied. Use the user's interests and access to propose a narrow question with a defensible geographic and time boundary. If you cannot inspect sources directly, ask for a catalogue description, finding aid, scan, transcription or source list that the user can provide. Use the first month to settle the research question, check source access, review background scholarship and identify the primary material needed. Keep a source log with author or creator, date, title, repository or publication, stable identifier and page or item locator when available. Check what the sources can actually answer before committing to the scope.

Use the second month to collect and compare evidence. Track which items were examined, the claims they support, conflicting accounts and gaps in coverage. Where feasible, compare independent sources and consider who created each record, for what purpose and what it leaves out. Distinguish documented facts, your interpretations and unresolved questions.

Use the third month to synthesize findings and write the report. Include the research question, scope and methods, findings organized around the evidence, and a brief discussion of limitations. Cite substantive factual claims using consistent Markdown notes or author-date references. Provide a bibliography with sufficient detail to locate each cited source. Before delivery, reconcile citations against the bibliography and spot-check key claims and quotations against the underlying sources. If access remains limited, document the gap and narrow the claims accordingly. Use a general local audience as a provisional default. Provide both deliverables in Markdown, as files if the host supports local file delivery or as copyable text otherwise.
